uncited: Marching Tetrahedra and Decomposition is an isosurface extraction method that resolves the topological ambiguities inherent in standard Marching Cubes by decomposing each cubic voxel into a fixed set of tetrahedra [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md].

Unlike Marching Cubes, which requires complex disambiguation logic for ambiguous cases, this method ensures a unique intersection topology for each of the 16 possible vertex configurations within a tetrahedron [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md].

It sets itself apart from its siblings by replacing the finite lookup table of configurations with a deterministic algorithm that reconstructs a local polygonal approximation given any number of intersections, and from [Error Analysis via Marching Tetrahedra](1308-error-analysis-via-marching-tetrahedra.md) by focusing on topological correctness and feature resolution rather than error bounds [1737-subgrid-marching-tetrahedra.md].

All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers.
**Surface Determination**: A criterion is applied to identify surface locations.
In isosurface methods, this involves comparing scalar values against a threshold (isovalue) to detect sign changes or equality [30-isosurface-extraction.md].
In blocky meshing, this involves checking occupancy states or material IDs to identify exposed boundaries [31-blocky-meshing.md].
**Mesh Coherence**: Adjacent primitives are merged or connected to form a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates and ensure watertightness [30-isosurface-extraction.md].

The method originates from the need to resolve the topological ambiguities present in the original Marching Cubes algorithm, which could produce non-manifold geometries in specific ambiguous cases [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md].
By decomposing the cube into tetrahedra, the problem is reduced to the 16 unambiguous cases of a tetrahedron [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md].
It is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization where topological correctness is critical [9029-marching-cubes-tetrahedron-decomposition.md].
